cards.title: Separating Incubation Stability from Pharmacodynamic Effect Delay
cards.claim: In an in vitro time-kill experiment, measure concentration stability before assuming constant exposure. If degradation is detected, obtain sufficient time-course measurements to characterize it; a first-order degradation model is a candidate only when supported. Evaluate a separate effect-delay component when concentration and killing trajectories support it, rather than forcing delay or degradation into every experiment.
conditions: Incubation concentration may change over the observation window.
The concentration assay and bacterial-count timing are documented.
required_inputs: Measured concentrations at the beginning and end of incubation and additional times when instability is suspected.
Time-matched bacterial counts, control growth and assay limits.
Candidate degradation and delay equations with units and parameter provenance.
limitations: First-order degradation is a model assumption, not a universal stability law.
Sparse observations can prevent estimation of a delay constant.
Improved fit does not independently identify the biological source of delay.
cards.downstream_use: Separate changing exposure from delayed response before interpreting potency or kill-rate estimates.

note: Method/reference scope retained; source identity is available in original evidence.
